newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany defends policy on Bosnian refugees.
newsitem.headline: Germany defends policy on Bosnian refugees.

text.p: Interior Minister Manfred Kanther defended Germany's controversial policy of forced repatriation of Bosnian refugees on Friday, but said those who had been ethnically cleansed would be treated with "sensitivity".

Speaking after a two-day meeting with interior ministers from Germany's 16 states, Kanther said they had agreed that deportations would go on but they would as a rule not deport Moslems or Croatians whose home areas are now Serb-dominated.

With poignant memories of the upheavals in their own country during World War Two, Germans took in some 320,000 refugees during the 1992-95 Bosnian war -- more than the rest of the European Union put together.
But since the Dayton peace accord 18 months ago the states have said they can no longer afford to keep the refugees and in October agreed to deport those who did not return voluntarily.
"The interior ministers have (however) agreed that refugees of Bosnian (Moslem) and Croatian origin from the Serb part of Bosnia required particular sensitivity," Kanther told a news conference.

The government ombudsman for foreigners' affairs, Cornelia Schmalz-Jacobson, criticised them in a statement for failing to establish clearly that "refugees' place of origin is the most important criterion" to determine their repatriation.
Bonn was appointing a coordinator to work with the Bosnian authorities and be based in Sarajevo to smooth repatriation, which refugee agencies say has been inconsistent and chaotic.

Kanther said Germany would nonetheless continue its policy of forced repatriation. He added that in any case it had hardly been applied and that only 269 had been deported, half of them convicted criminals.

"We deport people to their homeland. There is nothing unprecedented about this, many countries do it. We send people to Sarajevo where they are given a new home according to age and ethnic origin," Kanther said. He said they were not being airlifted back to their villages.

Gerhard Glogowski, Interior Minister for the state of Lower Saxony, accused the Bosnian authorities of not doing enough to help implement the Dayton peace accord and faciliate the refugees' return: "If they are getting our (European Union) money for reconstruction they must do something to deserve it".

Glogowski denied reports that traumatised refugees, who had been tortured or raped during the war, were being deported back to Bosnia. "There has not been one single case of this kind," he told the news conference.

Defence Minister Volker Ruehe offered the assistance of German troops in the multinational SFOR force in Bosnia to help refugees return to their homes. He said in a statement a coordination group of about 50 soldiers would gather information in various areas and lend returnees a helping hand.
Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel issued a statement welcoming the interior ministers' resolve to heed warnings about sending back refugees who had been expelled from their homes.
"We all agree the refugees must return. Bosnia is their home. They are desperately needed to reconstruct their homeland. But we can't afford to keep them forever," Kinkel said.
"We were humane to take them in, we must remain so in sending them home," said Kinkel, who has severely criticised Kanther and the states for their forced repatration scheme.
